content: The sensitivity and specificity of cytology followed by colposcopy, with or without biopsy, were calculated based on the diagnostic accuracy of these two tests. However, direct data were not available, and the estimates were derived indirectly. The variability in sensitivity and specificity for HPV testing and cytology (ASCUS) was notable, even when similar cut-off values were used. This inconsistency could not be attributed to the quality of the studies. Consequently, the evidence was downgraded due to imprecision and other factors. The wide confidence intervals (CIs) for sensitivity and specificity of cytology followed by colposcopy, and subsequently for true positives (TP), true negatives (TN), false positives (FP), and false negatives (FN), could lead to different clinical decisions depending on the assumed confidence limits. This highlights the uncertainty in the diagnostic accuracy of these methods. GRADE evidence for patient-important outcomes, such as mortality and morbidity, was assessed for various screen-and-treat strategies. HPV testing, with or without cryotherapy, LEEP, or CKC, was compared to cytology followed by colposcopy and biopsy when indicated. The outcomes included cervical cancer mortality, incidence, CIN2+ recurrence, undetected CIN2+ cases, major bleeding, premature delivery, infertility, major infections, minor infections, and unnecessary treatments. The data were presented per 100,000 patients screened. For cervical cancer mortality, the no screen group had the highest mortality (250 deaths per 100,000), while HPV-based strategies showed lower mortality rates (30–120 deaths per 100,000). Cervical cancer incidence was also highest in the no screen group (350 cases per 100,000) and lowest with HPV-based strategies (20–228 cases per 100,000). Recurrence of CIN2+ was highest in the no screen group (13,400 cases per 100,000) and varied across other strategies (1,677–8,888 cases per 100,000). Undetected CIN2+ cases (FN) were significant in some strategies, with up to 6,000 cases per 100,000 in certain HPV-based approaches. Major bleeding was most common with CKC (up to 4,100 cases per 100,000) and less frequent with other treatments. Premature delivery was observed in 500–564 cases per 100,000 across strategies, with no significant differences. Infertility data were not identified. Major infections were rare but occurred in up to 1,104 cases per 100,000 with CKC. Minor infections were more frequent, with up to 10,936 cases per 100,000 in CKC-treated populations. Unnecessary treatments (FP) were highest in HPV-based strategies (up to 8,000 cases per 100,000). The evidence quality for these outcomes was very low, primarily due to the low quality of data on treatment effects and the natural progression of CIN2+. The link between diagnostic test accuracy and treatment effects was also highly uncertain. The assumptions for mortality and incidence were based on data from Eastern Africa, with an age-standardized cervical cancer rate of 350 cases per 100,000 women and a CIN2+ pretest probability of 2%. The expert panel recommended a screen-and-treat strategy using VIA followed by cryotherapy (or LEEP when cryotherapy is not feasible) over cytology followed by colposcopy and biopsy. This recommendation was based on fewer harms associated with VIA, despite overtreatment and fewer cancers detected at first-time screening. Cytology-based programs require more resources due to quality control, training, and the need for a second visit. The recommendation applies to all women, regardless of HIV status, and is particularly relevant for countries considering or implementing these strategies.
